prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

﻿When it is cold it stinks, and not till then. The seasonable or more rabid heats Of love and summer in some other cities Unseal the all too human: not in his. When it is cold it stinks, but not before; Smells to high heaven then most creaturely When it is cold. It stinks, but not before His freezing eye has done its best to maim, To amputate limbs, livelihood and name, Abstracting life beyond all likelihood. When it is cold it stinks, and not till then Can it be fragrant. On canal and street, Colder and colder, Murphy to Molloy, The weather hardens round the Idiot Boy, The gleeful hero of the long retreat. When he is cold he stinks, but not before, This living corpse. The existential weather Smells out in these abortive minims, men Who barely living therefore altogether Live till they die; and sweetly smell till then.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: When, The, Unseal

outputs.L1:
When it is cold, it stinks—and not till then.  
The seasonable, or more rabid, heats  
Of love and summer in some other cities  
Unseal the all-too-human; not in his.  

When it is cold, it stinks, but not before;  
It smells to high heaven, then most creaturely,  
When it is cold. It stinks, but not before  
His freezing eye has done its best to maim,  
To amputate limbs, livelihood, and name,  
Abstracting life beyond all likelihood.  

When it is cold, it stinks—and not till then  
Can it be fragrant. On canal and street,  
Colder and colder, Murphy to Molloy,  
The weather hardens round the Idiot Boy,  
The gleeful hero of the long retreat.  

When he is cold, he stinks, but not before—  
This living corpse. The existential weather  
Smells out in these abortive minims: men  
Who, barely living, therefore altogether  
Live till they die—and sweetly smell till then.
outputs.L2:
Only with the arrival of cold does the stench emerge. Elsewhere, the timely—or more violent—fires of passion and summer expose what is excessively human, but not in his world. Here, no odor rises until the temperature falls. Then, in the frost, the body’s animal nature reeks all the way to heaven.

The smell begins only after his icy gaze has inflicted its worst: crippling bodies, cutting away limbs, livelihoods, and identities, and reducing life to an almost impossible abstraction. Only in coldness can the foulness become a kind of perfume.

Across canals and streets, the chill steadily deepens. From Murphy through Molloy, the climate closes and hardens around the Idiot Boy, the delighted champion of a prolonged withdrawal. This animate cadaver does not stink until he himself grows cold.

Such existential weather detects its own odor in these stunted little beings—men whose lives are so slight that, precisely because they scarcely live, they live completely until death comes, giving off sweetness up to that final moment.
outputs.L3:
The poem suggests that the city reveals its most intimate human and animal odors not in the heat of summer, as one might expect, but in the cold. Winter strips away the city’s disguises, exposing the vulnerability of the bodies that inhabit it. Its freezing, hostile gaze does more than observe: it maims, depriving people of their physical integrity, their livelihoods, their names, and even their sense of being alive.

As the weather hardens over canals and streets, figures such as Murphy, Molloy, and the Idiot Boy withdraw into a bleak, marginal existence. They inhabit a world defined by exposure, deprivation, and existential exhaustion. The poem presents them as “living corpses,” people reduced to the bare minimum of life, surviving without security, identity, or hope. Yet their condition is not simply one of defeat. However diminished they may be, they endure completely until death. Even amid bodily decay and spiritual desolation, they retain a paradoxical sweetness—a fragile trace of humanity that persists when almost everything else has been taken away.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents human existence at its most abject, exploring dehumanization and existential suffering through a series of recurring sensory images. Cold, stench, bodily mutilation, and decay reduce the figures in the poem to what appear to be “living corpses”: beings stripped of comfort, identity, social value, and almost every outward sign of ordinary humanity. The emphasis on damaged bodies and repellent smells forces the reader to confront a world in which people are treated as refuse. Physical deprivation thus becomes inseparable from spiritual and social exclusion.

The allusions to Beckett’s *Murphy* and *Molloy*, as well as to the Idiot Boy, place these figures within a tradition of marginal, wandering, or radically vulnerable characters. Like Beckett’s protagonists, they inhabit a condition in which conventional purposes and stable identities have broken down. Their lives may appear absurd, degraded, or emptied of meaning, yet their continued existence challenges any easy distinction between a valuable life and a worthless one. The poem’s repetition intensifies this challenge: cold and stench are not merely descriptive details but signs of a condition from which there seems to be no escape.

Yet the poem does not finally accept society’s dehumanizing judgment. Instead, it creates a paradox. Those who have been reduced most completely to bare life become, in their persistence, the most recognizably human. Their endurance requires no heroic gesture or reassuring explanation; simply remaining alive becomes an assertion of dignity. In this sense, the poem transforms its imagery of smell. The bodies condemned as foul or decaying become figuratively “fragrant,” because their vulnerability reveals a humanity more authentic than the values by which they have been rejected.

The poem therefore locates dignity not in beauty, health, usefulness, or social recognition, but in the stubborn continuation of life under extreme deprivation. Even when a person has been treated as a corpse before death, something irreducibly human remains. That humanity survives in the body’s persistence, in its exposure to pain, and in its refusal—or inability—to disappear. Only death finally ends this endurance. Until then, the poem suggests, even the most damaged and abandoned life retains a profound moral presence.
outputs.L5:
### When the Unseal

When the final lock gives way, the world will not end with thunder. The unseal will begin quietly: a whispered truth, a forgotten door opening, a light appearing beneath the walls we built around ourselves.

The past will step forward, carrying its secrets. Some will bring sorrow; others, freedom. In that moment, we will understand that not everything hidden was meant to remain buried.

When the unseal comes, courage will not mean standing without fear. It will mean opening what has long been closed—and choosing to face whatever waits beyond.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem about Samuel Beckett’s bleak fictional world, using cold weather, decay, and characters such as Murphy, Molloy, and the Idiot Boy as recurring images.
counterfactuals.output:
### **Zero Weather**

Snow worries the window,  
then forgets why.  
The road stiffens into a question  
no foot can finish.

Murphy rocks in the cold room,  
bound to his chair and the small black weather  
inside his skull.  
The fire has gone out politely.  
Ash keeps its appointment.

Molloy passes—or does not pass—  
beneath trees rotted hollow,  
his bicycle rusting beside him  
like a second skeleton.  
In his pockets, stones exchange  
their tasteless silences.

And the Idiot Boy comes again,  
blue with moonlight,  
carrying a broken pail  
through fields where nothing grows  
but frost and old mistakes.

The houses stoop.  
Their plaster loosens in the wind.  
A door swings open, shuts,  
opens—  
practicing departure.

Murphy counts the flakes.  
Molloy counts the stones.  
The Idiot Boy counts nothing,  
and so arrives first  
at the ditch where evening lies  
with weeds in its mouth.

No one asks for spring.  
They have heard of it, perhaps—  
a rumor among roots,  
a green fraud under the snow.

Night lowers its empty bucket.  
The stars corrode.  
Far off, a voice begins again  
the sentence it cannot complete.

Murphy rocks.  
Molloy crawls.  
The Idiot Boy crosses the white field,  
small as the last warm thought  
in a world determined  
to forget it.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a densely allusive critical poem in the style of mid-20th-century formal verse, exploring how existential cold strips Beckett’s characters of body, identity, and livelihood.
counterfactuals.output:
### **Zero at the Bone: Beckett’s Poor**

The climate is a creditor: it takes  
The coat from Murphy, marrow from Molloy;  
Along the road, beneath the whitest brakes,  
A name wears thin, a body loses joy.  
The bicycle rusts upright in the ditch;  
The beggar’s stone turns sacramental bread.  
No Lazarus is raised; the poor stay poor—  
Their alms, a boot; their patrimony, dread.

Malone inventories his little lease:  
A pencil, stick, and stories going numb.  
The room contracts. Each article of peace  
Is pawned to frost; the final figures come.  
Outside, Cartesian snow erases trade,  
The hand its craft, the mouth its former claim;  
Cogito cracks—the ghost is underpaid,  
And “I” becomes the alias of a name.

At Godot’s tree, two salaries of hope  
Fall due at dusk; the master and the slave  
Exchange their rope, their carrot, and their trope,  
While heaven keeps the silence of the grave.  
Poor Christ, poor Job, poor Chaplin in the cold—  
Their comic business shelters no one long:  
A hat passed round comes back with nothing told;  
The joke eats both the hunger and the tongue.

In Hamm’s blind kingdom, Clov attends the zero;  
Nagg and Nell lodge dustward in their bins.  
No throne survives except the chair of Nero,  
No wage but habit, paid in ancient sins.  
The world, that bankrupt firm, has closed its door;  
The sea itself is lead, the grain is gone.  
King Lear has dwindled to a kitchen chore,  
And Prospero dismisses no one—on.

Krapp warms the dark with vintages of breath,  
Rewinding youth to hear what youth mislaid;  
The spool, a little factory of death,  
Employs the voice whose speaker has decayed.  
And Winnie, gilded debtor of the sun,  
Sinks through the ledger—waist, then breast, then chin—  
Still crying “happy,” as if words, once spun,  
Could clothe the naked vacancy within.

Last, the Unnamable: no face, no post,  
No hand to beg with, nor a street to roam—  
A mouth foreclosed upon, a tenant ghost,  
Evicted even from the dream of home.  
Thus cold completes what history began:  
First work, then flesh, then proper noun withdrawn.  
Yet speech, that last poor matchstick of the man,  
Burns without heat—and cannot not burn on.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a dark, sonnet-like literary pastiche built around the refrain “When it is cold it stinks,” with references to canals, streets, living corpses, and abortive human lives.
counterfactuals.output:
Along the canals, beneath the iron sky,  
The drowned lamps shiver where the black scum drinks;  
A barge drifts past, as mute as God’s reply—  
**When it is cold it stinks.**

The streets cough up their living corpses, bowed,  
Who trade their names for bread, their blood for ink;  
Each face, half-born, dissolves into the crowd—  
**When it is cold it stinks.**

Abortive human lives knock at the gate,  
Brief sparks extinguished on oblivion’s brink;  
The clocks chew bone, the gutters whisper fate—  
**When it is cold it stinks.**

Yet dawn comes pale, ashamed of what it brings:  
A frozen bell, a throat of rust, that rings—  
**When it is cold it stinks.**
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Turn an analysis of Beckett’s fiction into verse: contrast love and summer with freezing abstraction, and portray his barely living protagonists as strangely fragrant until death.
counterfactuals.output:
Love comes in summer, warm with names,  
with hands that briefly make a home.  
Then thought blows in—white, absolute—  
and strips the flowering world to bone.  

His creatures crouch beside their breath,  
half ash, half appetite, confined;  
yet from their rags a strange scent rises—  
wet earth, old roses, ruined time.  

They scarcely live. They wait, diminish,  
while frost perfects its faceless art.  
Still, fragrant at the edge of nothing,  
they sweeten death before they depart.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a rhymed poem about existential alienation in Beckett, mentioning Murphy and Molloy and repeatedly linking coldness with stench, mutilation, retreat, and survival.
counterfactuals.output:
In Beckett’s dusk, where nameless shadows meet,  
The body fails, the mind denies defeat;  
Cold is the stench where the maimed selves retreat,  
Cold is survival, still dragging its feet.  

Murphy sits bound, aspiring to be still,  
Estranged from flesh, from charity, from will;  
Cold is the stench where the maimed selves retreat,  
Cold is survival, still dragging its feet.  

Molloy crawls onward, emptied of his way,  
His stones and crutches counting down the day;  
Cold is the stench where the maimed selves retreat,  
Cold is survival, still dragging its feet.  

Each word cuts off a limb it cannot name,  
Each silence shelters one exhausted flame;  
Cold is the stench where the maimed selves retreat,  
Cold is survival, still dragging its feet.  

No home endures, no whole self can be found,  
Just severed voices circling barren ground;  
Cold is the stench where the maimed selves retreat,  
Cold is survival, still dragging its feet.  

Yet through the void, though every nerve says cease,  
They limp beyond the counterfeit of peace;  
Cold is the stench where the maimed selves retreat,  
Cold is survival, still dragging its feet.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
